claims.text: Al and Ti are low-density, oxidation-active alloying elements.
Increasing Al or Ti content promotes controlled local elemental segregation.
Increasing Al or Ti content produces lattice distortions.
Local segregation of oxidation-active elements triggers formation of a coherent, protective high-temperature oxide scale such as Al2O3.
Alloying-induced lattice distortion enhances solid-solution strengthening by increasing resistance to dislocation motion.
Nanoprecipitation may contribute to strengthening in the modified alloy.
The proposed segregation, oxide formation, and strengthening mechanisms can enable low density, high strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance in one alloy.
The starting lightweight HEA is a uniform, single-phase solid solution containing refractory and low-density elements.
The controlled intervention is to increase Al or Ti content relative to a lower-Al/Ti baseline alloy while otherwise using identical processing.
During exposure, Al or Ti segregates to surfaces and grain boundaries.
Segregation and lattice distortion promote nucleation of coherent protective oxide nanoprecipitates.
The resulting coherent and adherent oxide scale reduces oxidation by acting as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
A stable oxide scale and homogenized microstructure enhance corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Relative to the baseline, the higher-Al/Ti alloy will form a more coherent protective oxide scale under oxidative and corrosive exposure.
Relative to the baseline, the higher-Al/Ti alloy will exhibit higher mechanical strength.
Relative to the baseline, the higher-Al/Ti alloy will exhibit a lower corrosion rate.
The mechanism should cease to provide benefits when rapid thermal cycling, reducing or non-oxidizing atmospheres, or kinetic limitations prevent segregation or disrupt oxide-scale formation.

Failure of the modified specimens to show statistically significant improvements in oxidation resistance, corrosion rate, and mechanical properties relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
